opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a pretty ambitious hope, and I'd put it somewhere in the range of, you know, maybe a 10 to 20 percent chance that it works out in the strong form we'd want. But I think it's worth taking seriously, and the reason is roughly this: when you train a neural network with gradient descent, you're doing a search over a huge space of programs and finding one that happens to perform well. And if it performs well, there's some reason it performs well. There's some structure in the data, some regularity in the world, that the model is exploiting. The hope is that the explanation for why the model behaves the way it does isn't fundamentally more complicated than the model itself. You found the model by search; maybe you can find the explanation by a comparable search, in parallel, at comparable cost.

The analogy I sometimes use is to mathematical proof. If you have a true conjecture, it's not obvious that there's a short proof. But in the case of neural nets, the "conjecture" is something like "this model gets low loss on the training distribution," and the reason that's true is precisely because gradient descent pushed it there. So there's a sense in which the training process itself is a kind of evidence, and we'd like to turn that evidence into an explanation, which is the thing we're trying to formalize with heuristic arguments rather than full proofs. Full proofs are almost certainly hopeless; neural nets are noisy and messy, and you're not going to prove anything airtight about them. But a heuristic explanation, something that says "here's the structure that accounts for this behavior, and here's why we'd expect it, absent something surprising," that seems more plausible.

Now, why might it fail? One worry is that some behaviors just don't have compact explanations. Maybe the model is doing something that only works because of a whole mess of coincidences, and the explanation is essentially "well, it's all these weights, and they happen to work." I think that's a real possibility. Another worry is that even if explanations exist, finding them could be much harder than finding the model, because gradient descent has this nice local structure and maybe the search for explanations doesn't. And a third worry is just that we don't yet know how to define what counts as an explanation in a way that's precise enough to optimize against. A lot of our work right now is on that last problem, trying to pin down what a heuristic argument even is formally.

So my overall view is that it's a long shot, but it's the kind of long shot where if it works, you get something really valuable: you can ask, for a given behavior of the model, "is this happening for the reason we think, or for some other reason?" That's exactly what you'd want for catching things like deceptive alignment or a model behaving well in training for bad reasons. And I think even partial progress, explanations that work for some fraction of behaviors or that are only approximately as cheap as training, could still be quite useful. So I'm excited enough about it to spend most of my time on it, while being pretty honest that the odds aren't great.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the central questions for whether the kind of research we're doing at ARC actually goes anywhere. The hope is something like: if gradient descent can find a network that behaves a certain way, then there should be some explanation of why it behaves that way, and finding that explanation shouldn't be astronomically harder than finding the network in the first place. I'd say I'm maybe 50/50 on something in that vicinity being true, and I want to be clear about why it's not obvious.

The pessimistic case is pretty simple. Learning is just search. You have a loss function, you have a bunch of parameters, you move downhill, and you end up somewhere that works. At no point does that process produce a reason the thing works. Nature does this all the time. Evolution found protein folding without ever producing a theory of protein folding, and we've spent decades trying to produce one after the fact. So there's no general principle that says "if you can find it, you can explain it." In fact, the default expectation from complexity theory is sort of the opposite: verifying or explaining can be strictly harder than searching, depending on what you mean by explain.

So why do I still have real hope? A few reasons. One is that the notion of explanation we're after is weaker than what people usually imagine. We're not looking for a human-readable story, or something you could write in a textbook. We're looking for a formal object, a kind of heuristic argument, that accounts for the network's behavior well enough that if the behavior changed in some rare case, the argument would have to change too. That's a much lower bar than full mechanistic understanding, and I think a lot of the intuition that "interpretability is hopeless" comes from imagining the higher bar.

The second reason is that gradient descent is doing something structured. The regularities the network exploits are regularities in the data, and the network has to represent them somehow in order to use them. Whatever structure makes the behavior work is, in some sense, already sitting in the weights. The question is whether you can read it out in a form that lets you make claims about behavior, rather than reconstructing it from scratch. And it's plausible that the reading-out is comparably hard to the writing-in, because they're sort of dual problems: in one case you're searching for parameters that make the loss go down, in the other you're searching for an argument that explains why the loss went down.

The third thing I'd say is that you don't have to find the explanation afterward. You can co-train. You can search for the model and the explanation of the model at the same time, and penalize models that don't come with explanations. That changes the game quite a bit. The question becomes "is the set of explainable models rich enough to contain good ones," rather than "can I explain an arbitrary thing gradient descent happened to produce." I think the first question is much more likely to have a good answer.

Where I'd really worry is if it turns out that the useful stuff models learn is fundamentally a huge pile of small, unrelated heuristics with no compressible structure. If that's the world, then any explanation is roughly as big as the network itself, and you haven't gained anything. I don't think that's the world, mostly because models generalize, and generalization suggests there's something more compact going on. But I hold that loosely.

So my honest assessment is: this is a research bet, not a confident prediction. If I had to put numbers on it, I'd say there's a decent chance the problem is tractable in the regime that matters, a decent chance it's tractable but only with techniques we don't have yet, and a real chance it's just not going to work and we'll need to lean much harder on other approaches. The reason I think it's worth working on anyway is that the payoff if it does work is enormous. You'd have a way to say something about what a model does on inputs you've never seen, and that's exactly the thing every other alignment approach is missing.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real possibility, but I don’t think we have a strong reason to expect it. There’s a distinction between understanding what a network is doing well enough to make useful predictions and finding a crisp explanation that lets you establish that it will behave correctly in all the cases you care about. The second thing could be much harder.

If you think about how humans solve problems, we can often learn to do something long before we can give a rigorous account of why it works. That doesn’t mean a rigorous account is impossible, but it makes me hesitant to assume that finding one costs about as much as learning the behavior in the first place.

The hope I find more plausible is that you don’t need to explain everything. You need to identify some particular properties that matter for safety, and perhaps those properties have relatively simple explanations even when the overall computation is complicated. Then the question is whether you can train systems in a way that makes those explanations available, without giving up too much of what made the systems useful. I think that’s a very interesting direction; I just wouldn’t want to count on it working.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real hope there, but I don’t think we have a strong reason to expect it to work. There’s a difference between finding a computation that performs well and finding an explanation of why that computation performs well. In general, the second problem could be much harder.

One reason for optimism is that these networks were found by gradient descent. They’re not arbitrary circuits someone constructed to be maximally inscrutable. Whatever structure makes them work had to be accessible to the training process. You might hope that gives us a way to recover an explanation with a comparable amount of effort.

But that’s not an argument that the explanation has to be short, or that it has to take a form humans can understand. You could imagine a network having a huge number of little heuristics that interact in complicated ways. Explaining all those interactions might effectively require reproducing the network.

So I’d distinguish understanding everything the model does from establishing some particular property we care about. Maybe a complete explanation is intractable, but we can still get a sufficiently good handle on why it won’t behave in some catastrophic way. That seems like a more plausible target to me, although it’s still a very open question how far we can get.
